ourAnswer: Two methyl free radicals produced in propagation combine in the chain-termination step: CH3 radical + CH3 radical gives CH3-CH3.
keyAnswer: Due to the side reaction in termination step by the combination of two CH3 free radicals.
note: Same mechanism, same step.

ourAnswer: (a) 2-Methylbut-2-ene (b) Pent-1-en-3-yne (c) Buta-1,3-diene (d) 4-Phenylbut-1-ene (e) 2-Methylphenol (f) 5-(2-Methylpropyl)decane (g) 4-Ethyldeca-1,5,8-triene
keyAnswer: (a) 2-Methyl-but-2-ene (b) Pent-1-ene-3-yne (c) Buta-1,3-diene (d) 4-Phenylbut-1-ene (e) 2-Methylphenol (f) 5-(2-Methylpropyl)-decane (g) 4-Ethyldeca-1,5,8-triene
note: All seven sub-items match; the only differences are hyphenation. This is the strongest single check in the chapter because (c), (d) and (e) had to be read off drawn structures and (f), (g) needed the parent chain and numbering to be worked out.

ourAnswer: (a) But-1-ene, But-2-ene, 2-Methylprop-1-ene. (b) Pent-1-yne, Pent-2-yne, 3-Methylbut-1-yne.
keyAnswer: (a) But-1-ene, But-2-ene, 2-Methylpropene. (b) Pent-1-yne, Pent-2-yne, 3-Methylbut-1-yne.
note: Three isomers each, all matching. 2-Methylprop-1-ene and 2-Methylpropene are the same compound (propene admits only one double-bond position, so the locant is redundant, not wrong). Separately, the key's PRINTED STRUCTURE for (a)(ii) reads CH3 - CH2 = CH - CH3, which is not but-2-ene and gives a pentavalent carbon; the name it prints alongside, But-2-ene, is correct. A drawing slip in the key, not an answer error.

ourAnswer: (i) Ethanal and Propanal (ii) Butan-2-one and Pentan-2-one (iii) Methanal and Pentan-3-one (iv) Benzaldehyde and Propanal
keyAnswer: (i) Ethanal and propanal (ii) Butan-2-one and pentan-2-one (iii) Methanal and pentan-3-one (iv) Propanal and benzaldehyde
note: All four pairs identical (the key lists (iv) in the reverse order).

ourAnswer: CH3-CH=C(C2H5)2; 3-Ethylpent-2-ene
keyAnswer: 3-Ethylpent-2-ene
note: Same compound and same name.

ourAnswer: But-2-ene
keyAnswer: But-2-ene
note: Bond count gives C4H8 with one C=C; two moles of a single aldehyde of M = 44 (ethanal) forces the symmetric CH3-CH=CH-CH3.

ourAnswer: CH3CH2-CH=C(C2H5)2, i.e. CH3CH2-C(C2H5)=CH-CH2CH3; named 3-Ethylhex-3-ene
keyAnswer: 4-Ethylhex-3-ene, drawn as CH3-CH2-C(=CH-CH2-CH3) carrying a CH2-CH3 branch
note: THE STRUCTURE AGREES EXACTLY - the key's drawn structure is the same molecule as ours, and the structural formula is the only thing the question asks for. The defect is in the NAME the key volunteers alongside it. The hexene chain can be numbered from either end and BOTH directions put the double bond at C-3, so that criterion is a tie; the tiebreak then goes to the lower locant for the detachable prefix, ethyl at 3 rather than 4. Hence 3-Ethylhex-3-ene, not 4-Ethylhex-3-ene. The book applies this tiebreak correctly elsewhere in the same chapter (Problem 9.7 (iv), where 4-Ethyl-2,6-dimethyldec-4-ene really is forced by the methyl locants). Low severity: no answer to the question as asked is affected.

All four equations agree (ours are the key's, doubled, in (i)-(iii)). The key's part (c) misprints hexyne's formula as C5H10, but its own coefficients - 17/2 O2 giving 6 CO2 + 5 H2O - are those of C6H10 and balance only for C6H10, so the formula is a typo and the equation is right. Recorded rather than scored as a defect because no answer changes.

ourAnswer: cis-hex-2-ene has the higher boiling point: in the cis form the two C-alkyl bond dipoles add to give a net dipole moment, so dipole-dipole attraction is stronger; in the trans form they nearly cancel.
keyAnswer: The cis form will have higher boiling point due to more polar nature leading to stronger intermolecular dipole-dipole interaction, thus requiring more heat energy to separate them.
note: Same isomer, same reason.

ourAnswer: Resonance: benzene is a hybrid of two equivalent Kekule structures, so its six pi electrons are fully delocalised, all six C-C bonds are equal at 139 pm, Huckel's 4n+2 rule is satisfied with n = 1, and the delocalisation energy is about 150 kJ/mol.
keyAnswer: Due to resonance
note: The key gives the one-word reason; ours is the same answer with the supporting evidence.

ourAnswer: Planar; complete delocalisation over an uninterrupted ring (every ring atom sp2 with a p orbital); (4n+2) pi electrons, n = 0, 1, 2, ... (Huckel's rule).
keyAnswer: Planar, conjugated ring system with delocalisation of (4n+2) electrons, where n is an integer
note: Same three conditions. The pi symbol does not render on the key's page - the same dropped-glyph fault the chapter shows elsewhere - but the sense is unambiguous.

ourAnswer: (i) an sp3 CH2 in the ring breaks the p-orbital circuit and the ring holds only 4 pi electrons (4n), with the third pi bond exocyclic; (ii) cyclopentadiene has an sp3 CH2 and only 4 pi electrons; (iii) cyclooctatetraene has 8 pi electrons (4n) and adopts a non-planar tub shape.
keyAnswer: Lack of delocalisation of (4n+2) pi electrons in the cyclic system.
note: The key gives one blanket reason covering all three; ours applies it system by system and adds the non-planarity of cyclooctatetraene. Same verdict for each.

ourAnswer: (i) Br2/anhyd. FeBr3 then conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4, separate the para isomer. (ii) nitrate FIRST (conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4), then Cl2/anhyd. FeCl3, giving m-nitrochlorobenzene. (iii) CH3Cl/anhyd. AlCl3 then conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4, separate the para isomer. (iv) CH3COCl/anhyd. AlCl3.
keyAnswer: (i) as ours, with separation by fractional distillation. (ii) benzene -> nitrobenzene -> Cl2/anhyd. AlCl3 -> a ring drawn bearing Br and Cl in the meta positions. (iii) as ours but with dil HNO3 + dil H2SO4. (iv) as ours.
note: TWO defects in the key, both in parts we agree with on route. (1) Part (ii): the final product is DRAWN as 1-bromo-3-chlorobenzene - a Br where the NO2 belongs. It is self-refuting: the scheme's own immediately preceding step produces nitrobenzene (drawn with NO2), and no bromine-containing reagent appears anywhere in the sequence, so the product can only be m-nitrochlorobenzene, which is what the question asks for. Verified at 5x magnification. (2) Part (iii) specifies dil HNO3 + dil H2SO4 for a ring nitration, where the key's own parts (i) and (ii) and the chapter text both use conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4. Our routes and products are correct in all four parts.

ourAnswer: Five 1-degree carbons with 3 H each (15 H); two 2-degree carbons with 2 H each (4 H); one 3-degree carbon with 1 H. (The remaining carbon is quaternary with no H.)
keyAnswer: 15 H attached to 1-degree carbons, 4 H attached to 2-degree carbons, 1 H attached to 3-degree carbons; structure labelled 1,2,4,2,3 along the chain with four 1-degree methyls.
note: Exact match, including the quaternary carbon our answer names in passing and the key labels 4-degree on its structure. Note the degree signs do not render on the QUESTION page (it prints 'identify 1 ,2 ,3 carbon atoms'), but they DO render in the key, which confirms the reading our _note recorded.

ourAnswer: Branching lowers the boiling point: a more compact, more spherical molecule has less surface area, so van der Waals forces weaken. Pentane 309 K > 2-methylbutane 301 K > 2,2-dimethylpropane 282.5 K.
keyAnswer: More the branching in alkane, lower will be the boiling point.
note: Same direction; ours adds the mechanism and the book's own C5H12 boiling points.

ourAnswer: Markovnikov ionic addition via the more stable secondary carbocation gives 2-bromopropane; with benzoyl peroxide a free radical chain in which Br adds first, via the more stable secondary radical, gives 1-bromopropane. Full initiation and propagation steps given for both.
keyAnswer: Refer to addition reaction of HBr to unsymmetrical alkenes in the text.
note: The key prints a cross-reference to the chapter rather than an answer, so there is nothing to diff and this row is EXCLUDED from the diffed denominator. Our answer follows exactly the mechanism the referenced text (Section 9.3.5, Markovnikov rule and peroxide effect) sets out, including the point that the peroxide effect is seen with HBr but not HCl or HI.

ourAnswer: Glyoxal (ethanedial), 2-oxopropanal (methylglyoxal) and butane-2,3-dione. No single Kekule structure can give all three, so o-xylene (and hence benzene) must be a hybrid of the two Kekule forms.
keyAnswer: CH3-CO-CO-CH3, CH3-CO-CHO and OHC-CHO. 'All the three products cannot be obtained by any one of the Kekule's structures. This shows that benzene is a resonance hybrid of the two resonating structures.'
note: The same three dicarbonyl products and the same inference, reached independently.

ourAnswer: Ethyne > Benzene > n-Hexane, on s character of the C-H carbon: sp 50%, sp2 33.3%, sp3 25%.
keyAnswer: H-C=C-H > C6H6 > C6H14, due to maximum s orbital character in ethyne (50 per cent) as compared to 33 per cent in benzene and 25 per cent in n-hexane.
note: Identical order and identical reason. (The key misspells ethyne as 'enthyne'.)

ourAnswer: The delocalised pi cloud makes the ring electron-rich and attracts electrophiles, and substitution preserves the aromatic sextet; the same high electron density repels nucleophiles, and there is no leaving group.
keyAnswer: Due to the presence of 6 pi electrons, benzene behaves as a rich source of electrons thus being easily attacked by reagents deficient in electrons.
note: The key answers only the electrophilic half of the question; ours agrees with it and additionally answers the nucleophilic half the question also asks.

ourAnswer: (i) 3 CH=CH, red hot iron tube at 873 K. (ii) ethene -> 1,2-dibromoethane (Br2) -> bromoethene (alc. KOH) -> ethyne (NaNH2) -> benzene (red hot iron tube, 873 K). (iii) n-hexane over Cr2O3/V2O5/Mo2O3 on alumina at 773 K and 10-20 atm.
keyAnswer: (i) 3 CH=CH, red hot iron tube 873 K. (ii) C2H4 -> CH2Br-CH2Br -> CH2=CHBr -> HC=CH -> benzene. (iii) C6H14 over Cr2O3/V2O5/Mo2O3 at 773 K, 10-20 atm.
note: All three routes identical, including the reagents and conditions. (The key prints 'CH2=CHNr' for CH2=CHBr, 'BR' for Br and '10-20 atom' for atm.)

ourAnswer: 2-Methylbut-1-ene, 2-Methylbut-2-ene, 3-Methylbut-1-ene.
keyAnswer: 2-Methylbut-1-ene, 2-Methylbut-2-ene, 3-Methylbut-1-ene.
note: Same three alkenes, same structures, same names, and both note that a double bond to the branch methyl duplicates 2-methylbut-1-ene.

ourAnswer: (a) Chlorobenzene > p-Nitrochlorobenzene > 2,4-Dinitrochlorobenzene. (b) Toluene > p-nitrotoluene > p-dinitrobenzene.
keyAnswer: (a) Chlorobenzene > p-nitrochlorobenzene > 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene. (b) Toluene > p-CH3-C6H4-NO2 > p-O2N-C6H4-NO2.
note: Both orders identical.

ourAnswer: Toluene, because the electron-releasing methyl group raises the ring's electron density and stabilises the arenium ion; full order Toluene > Benzene > m-Dinitrobenzene.
keyAnswer: Toluene undergoes nitration most easily due to electron releasing nature of the methyl group.
note: Same compound, same reason. (The key misspells 'Toleune'.)

ourAnswer: Anhydrous FeCl3 (also FeBr3, BF3 or SnCl4).
keyAnswer: FeCl3
note: Same Lewis acid; ours also gives the equation for how it generates the ethyl carbocation.

ourAnswer: A single alkyl halide can only give an even-carbon alkane, so an odd-carbon alkane needs two different halides and then all three couplings occur, giving a mixture with poor yield. Example: CH3Br + C2H5Br + 2Na gives propane alongside ethane and n-butane.
keyAnswer: Due to the formation of side products. For example, by starting with 1-bromopropane and 1-bromobutane, hexane and octane are the side products besides heptane.
note: Same principle and same three-product outcome; the question asks for one example and the two examples chosen differ (ours propane from C1 + C2, the key's heptane from C3 + C4). Both are valid illustrations.
